extracted.intended_audience: regulated industry (EGU owners/operators), state permitting authorities, EPA reviewers, and other stakeholders participating in EPA air rulemaking and compliance planning
extracted.subtask_short: EPA BSER for CCS on turbines
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and evaluative standards the EPA used in the preamble to determine that carbon capture and sequestration (CCS) at 90% capture is part of the Best System of Emission Reduction (BSER) for new base-load combined cycle combustion turbines, including cost, demonstration, impacts, timelines, and regulatory safeguards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequately demonstrated technology
rubrics_metrics.description: Under CAA section 111, a control technology must be 'adequately demonstrated' for affected sources to qualify as BSER.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA explains that adequacy does not require widespread commercial use nationally; it must be demonstrated for affected sources and deployable at scale within the compliance timeframe. The preamble rejects arguments that lack of immediate widespread deployment means CCS is not adequately demonstrated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost-reasonableness of CCS
rubrics_metrics.description: The costs of implementing CCS must be reasonable and comparable to costs the EPA has required in prior rules for fossil-fuel electric generating units.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA amortizes costs over expected operating life (30 years), models scenarios (continued capture operation vs. not operating capture after tax-credit period), compares compliance costs ($/MWh and $/ton) for representative H-Class and F-Class turbines to prior rule metrics, and concludes CCS costs are reasonable. EPA also models conservative and adjusted cost reductions (e.g., 5% lower) to reflect likely efficiency and technological improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of IRC section 45Q tax credit in cost analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA incorporates the revised IRC section 45Q tax credit ($85/metric ton) into its CCS cost calculations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because 45Q is available for 12 years after operation begins, EPA models higher capacity factors and revenues during that period and lower ones afterwards; recognizes the tax credit substantially offsets capture/transport/sequestration costs and affects dispatch behavior and amortized cost calculations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity factor and operational scenario assumptions
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA uses specific capacity factor assumptions to estimate deployment economics, e.g., 80% during initial 12-year tax-credit period and 31% during the subsequent 18 years (30-year average 51%).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA evaluated multiple operational scenarios, including constant generation at 60–80% over 30 years, and shows how higher capacity factors reduce per-ton costs. It notes subcategorization consequences (e.g., 31% would classify unit as intermediate-load) and provides two CCS cost sets (continued vs. discontinued operation after 12 years).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of NETL/DOE models and guidance for transport/sequestration costs
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA relies on NETL's 'Quality Guidelines for Energy System Studies' and the CO2 Transport Cost Model for estimating pipeline transport and sequestration costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The NETL guidelines estimate single point-to-point pipeline capital, related capital expenditures, O&M, site screening, permitting, injection wells/equipment, pore volume acquisition, long-term liability protection, and factor in UIC Class VI and GHGRP subpart RR regulatory requirements; NETL calculates sequestration costs for generic plant locations (Midwest, Texas, ND, MT).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of primary sequestration cost drivers
rubrics_metrics.description: Cost drivers for CO2 sequestration projects include the injection rate and the areal extent of the CO2 plume in the reservoir.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA explains that injection rate depends on reservoir thickness and permeability (thick, permeable reservoirs need fewer wells), and areal extents depend on sequestration capacity (thick, porous reservoirs with good sequestration coefficient have smaller plume area and lower testing/monitoring costs). NETL models costs on cumulative storage potential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of learning rates and projected cost declines
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA assesses evidence that CCS costs have been declining and projects further reductions driven by technological learning and deployment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites studies showing learning rates (5–27% for capital and O&M for analogous technologies), historical capture-cost declines (e.g., $95/ton in older studies to ~$50/ton by 2025 estimates), DOE/NREL/EIA modeled reductions (EIA assumes minimum 20% reduction by 2035; NREL projects 10% capex reduction 2021–2032 under conservative scenario), and DOE case studies using 25% capex reduction for Nth-of-a-Kind facilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison to other control costs (benchmarking)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA compares CCS costs for representative new base-load combustion turbines to costs of other controls it has required and to other greenhouse gas control costs to determine reasonableness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA states CCS costs are generally lower than costs of other controls in prior EPA rules for fossil- fuel EGUs, supporting the finding that CCS costs are reasonable in this rulemaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of non-air quality health and environmental impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA evaluates non-air quality health and environmental impacts (energy requirements, non-GHG emissions, water use) and concludes CCS has limited consequences in these areas for new combined cycle turbines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA discusses increased parasitic/auxiliary energy demand and de-rating, non-GHG pollutant formation and mitigation, water use increases and mitigations (dry/hybrid cooling), and concludes these impacts are limited and do not disqualify CCS as BSER.

rubrics_metrics.name: Energy requirements: de-rating and scaling options
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA recognizes that installing a ≥90% carbon capture system increases parasitic energy demand and reduces net power output (de-rating), but considers scaling larger to accommodate CCS feasible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides example: a 500 MWe-net plant would be de-rated by 11% (to 444 MWe-net) with CCS, or developers can build a larger 563 MWe-net plant so CCS-equipped unit still delivers 500 MWe-net. EPA deems scaling a viable option.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of CCS on criteria air pollutant emissions
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA finds the installation and operation of CCS itself does not impact a unit's potential-to-emit criteria air pollutants, though scaling larger could increase emissions which are subject to other CAA controls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA notes emission rates for non-GHG pollutants from natural gas turbines are relatively low; mitigation controls (BACT, LAER, NSR requirements) and other pollution controls typically address any increases from scaling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigation and control of amine degradation products and HAPs
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA requires consideration of mitigation for amine solvent degradation products (e.g., nitrosamines) and listed HAPs such as formaldehyde and acetaldehyde when CCS systems are major HAP sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A conventional multistage water wash or acid wash and a mist eliminator (demister) at CO2 scrubber exit effectively remove gaseous amine and degradation products. EPA also notes selection of compatible materials and interstage cooling limit solvent oxidation; where applicable, section 112(g)/MACT analyses should be conducted on case-by-case basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Water use impacts and mitigation
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA assesses cooling-water requirements: combined cycle EGU without CCS needs ~190 gallons/MWh; with CCS needs ~290 gallons/MWh (≈50% increase), but absolute increase is small relative to coal-fired EGUs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA notes many combined cycle EGUs use dry cooling and that dry or hybrid cooling for CO2 capture would reduce additional water needs; concludes increased water requirements are addressable and do not disqualify CCS from BSER.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of community and environmental justice concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA considers stakeholder concerns that historically disadvantaged and overburdened communities may bear disproportionate burdens from CCS projects and incorporates these considerations into analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA references its analysis in section XII.E, commits to meaningful engagement requirements (section X.E.1.b.i), public notice/comment requirements for permits, and expects project developers and permitting authorities to consider community concerns; EPA regional offices will review CO2 capture permits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on regulatory frameworks to manage CCS risks
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA emphasizes existing regulatory programs (NSR/BACT/LAER, PHMSA pipeline oversight, UIC Class VI, GHGRP) provide protections for public health, safety, and the environment in CCS projects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Projects subject to major NSR must apply BACT for attainment pollutants and LAER/offsets for nonattainment pollutants; PHMSA oversees pipeline safety; UIC Class VI and GHGRP subpart RR protect USDWs and ensure geologic sequestration security.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promotion of technology development and spillover benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA considers whether designating CCS as part of BSER will promote further technological development and broader implementation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA concludes the standard—combined with 45Q and IIJA investments—should incentivize better solvents/components and advance capture tech for lower CO2 concentration sources (e.g., enabling retrofits of existing combined cycle EGUs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance date feasibility and limited extension mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA sets a final compliance date (January 1, 2032) for the phase 2 CCS standard and provides for up to a 1-year compliance-date extension where delays are beyond the EGU owner's control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA considered comments on proposed dates, project timelines (Sargent & Lundy baseline ~6.25 years; extended schedule ~7 years), and alignment with timelines for coal-fired EGUs; final date allows >7 years for many sources that commenced construction prior to rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Project timeline assumptions based on industry studies
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA bases CCS project schedule expectations on the Sargent & Lundy capture plant schedule and related analyses for coal-fired steam generating units, applying extended timelines (~7 years) for new combustion turbines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA explains new sources can begin substantial work earlier (FEED, right-of-way) but notes some state-plan-related mechanisms (e.g., RULOF) don't apply to new sources; timelines drive reasonable compliance-date determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowance of alternative compliance pathways
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA permits other compliance options for meeting performance standards—for example, constructing units designed to co-fire low-GHG hydrogen sufficient to meet the standard instead of CCS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA notes industry is pursuing both CCS-equipped units and hydrogen co-firing projects; offering alternative pathways reduces reliability concerns associated with designating CCS as part of BSER.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipated infrastructure investments and policy supports (IIJA/IRA)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA accounts for IIJA and IRA provisions that increase investments in CO2 transport infrastructure, sequestration site development, and enhanced 45Q tax credits, which are expected to reduce CCS costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IIJA programs referenced include Carbon Dioxide Transportation Infrastructure Finance and Innovation (loans/grants), Regional Direct Air Capture Hubs, and DOE's CarbonSAFE initiative; IRA enhances 45Q—these supports are expected to accelerate deployment and reduce costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of conservative assumptions in cost estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA describes its CCS cost estimates as conservatively high because they exclude certain potential efficiency improvements and post-credit revenue streams.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA did not account for exhaust gas recirculation (which could lower LCOE ~3.4%), potential efficiency improvements for combined cycle units, or possible CO2 sales/revenue after 45Q expires; EPA also presents costs with an assumed 5% reduction to approximate likely improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantification of emission reduction effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA quantifies expected CO2 reductions from implementing 90% capture CCS on base-load combined cycle EGUs (e.g., avoids ~41 million tons CO2 over 30 years for a representative unit).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA notes adding 90% capture increases gross heat rate by 7% and net heat rate by 13%, so gross/net emissions rates reduce by ~89.3% and ~88.7% respectively (not a one-to-one 90% reduction due to auxiliary energy use); reductions are larger than other industrial sources except coal-fired steam units.
